Histolytica trophozoite (20-40 µm, haematophagous, invasive), minuta (10-15 µm, commensal), cyst (10-15 µm, 4 nuclei, infective, chlorine-resistant).

Within 5 months in 95%; Fontan triad: fever 39-40 °C, painful hepatomegaly, RUQ pain; anchovy-sauce pus; emergency.

No vaccine; hand washing, wash fruit and vegetables, boil or filter water, sanitation, health education.

body.back: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. In profound, prolonged neutropenia or steroids; fever resistant to antibiotics > 4 days; halo sign on CT.
Diseases due to cosmopolitan opportunistic filamentous fungi (Aspergillus): immunoallergic, localised (aspergilloma) or invasive forms.
Hyaline septate hyphae; aspergillary head: conidiophore, vesicle ± metulae, phialides, chains of conidia; A. fumigatus 90%.
Environmental (construction), local (cavities, smoking, cystic fibrosis, radiotherapy), general (neutropenia < 500, steroids, CGD).
Extrinsic allergic alveolitis (precipitins, farmer's lung), aspergillary asthma (IgE), ABPA (eosinophilia > 1000, high IgE, plugs).
Fungus ball in a pre-existing cavity communicating with a bronchus; air-crescent/bell sign; haemoptysis; surgery.
Neutropenia > 10 days, steroids, transplants; fever resistant to antibiotics > 4 days, chest pain; CT halo then air crescent; high mortality.
Direct exam, culture (Sabouraud 37 °C, 3-4 days), MALDI-TOF, galactomannan (serum/BAL), β-D-glucan, histology (PAS, silver), PCR.
Proven (histology with tissue damage or sterile-site culture), probable (host + clinical + mycological), possible (host + clinical, no mycology).
Voriconazole (reference), other azoles, liposomal amphotericin, echinocandins; surgery for aspergilloma; sterile rooms, HEPA, posaconazole prophylaxis.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Miracidium. Ciliated embryo hatching in warm, lit fresh water to find its snail.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intermediate host. Freshwater snails: Bulinus for S. haematobium, Biomphalaria (planorbis) for S. mansoni, Oncomelania for S. japonicum.

title: Four human schistosomes and snail hosts?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Four human schistosomes and snail hosts?
body.back: S. haematobium (urogenital, Bulinus), S. mansoni (intestinal, Biomphalaria), S. japonicum (intestinal, Oncomelania), S. intercalatum (rectal/genital, Bulinus).
Only S. haematobium; since 1927, south of the Atlas (Errachidia, Zagora, Agadir), Ouarzazate dam outbreak; some northern foci.
Separate sexes; male with gynaecophoric canal holding the female; two suckers; eggs embryonated with a spine.
Haematobium: oval, large terminal. Mansoni: oval, large lateral. Intercalatum: rhomboid, terminal. Japonicum: round, small lateral.
Egg → miracidium in fresh water → snail → cercaria → skin penetration → schistosomule → adults in venous plexus → eggs excreted or trapped (granulomas).
Penetration: cercarial dermatitis. Invasion (5-6 weeks): fever, allergy, eosinophilia. State: haematuria/cystitis (haematobium) or dysentery, liver fibrosis (mansoni).
From 6-8 weeks: urine at noon after exercise (haematobium), stool with Kato, rectal/bladder biopsy; live egg = active; dead/calcified = old.
Positive 15-30 days after infection; useful in invasion, chronic phase, follow-up; rises after treatment, negative after 12-15 months.
Praziquantel single-day course: 40 mg/kg (haematobium, mansoni, intercalatum), 60 mg/kg (japonicum); well tolerated, mass treatment.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diagnosis. Direct exam, culture on Sabouraud and chromogenic media, germ-tube test for C. albicans, mannan and β-glucan antigens.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Systemic candidiasis. Candidaemia, endophthalmitis, endocarditis, hepatosplenic, bone, brain and urinary candidiasis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mucosal candidiasis. Oral thrush, oesophageal candidiasis (HIV with CD4 < 100), vulvovaginal candidiasis (75% of women).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Contributing factors. Newborns, elderly, pregnancy, moisture, dentures, diabetes, neutropenia, HIV; antibiotics, steroids, catheters, surgery, burns.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cutaneous and nail. Intertrigo of large and small folds, napkin candidiasis, perionyxis leading to onyxis.
Cosmopolitan infections by Candida yeasts arising with local or general immunodeficiency: superficial mucocutaneous or deep/disseminated.
C. albicans (main, commensal); C. glabrata, tropicalis, krusei, parapsilosis, dubliniensis, auris.
Host: newborns, elderly, pregnancy, moisture, dentures, diabetes, neutropenia, HIV. Iatrogenic: antibiotics, steroids, catheters, parenteral nutrition, surgery, burns.
Oral thrush (CD4 < 300), oesophageal (CD4 < 100; dysphagia), digestive, vulvovaginal (75% of women; curd-like discharge), balanitis.
Intertrigo of large/small folds with satellite pustules, napkin candidiasis, perionyxis → onyxis of fingernails.
Candidaemia, endophthalmitis, endocarditis, hepatosplenic, bone, brain, urinary, pneumonia; proven/probable/possible criteria.
Direct exam (budding yeasts), Sabouraud/chromogenic culture, germ-tube test, latex, chlamydospores on RAT/PCB.
Oral: local amphotericin/nystatin/miconazole, fluconazole if recurrent. Skin: local azoles/terbinafine. Nail: local + systemic. Invasive: echinocandins, fluconazole, amphotericin B, voriconazole.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Blastocystis hominis. Colonic protozoan; pathogenic when numerous (> 5 per field), in children, elderly and HIV; metronidazole.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cryptosporidium. C. hominis and C. parvum; oocysts infective at once, resist chlorination; waterborne epidemics; chronic in AIDS (CD4 < 100).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Coccidian cycle. Asexual schizogony in enterocytes, sexual gamogony, then sporogony giving the oocyst shed in stool.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cyclospora cayetanensis. Tropical; oocysts must mature outside; raspberries, strawberries, basil; watery traveller's diarrhoea; cotrimoxazole.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Isospora belli. Tropical, strictly human, opportunistic; watery diarrhoea with fever 39-40 °C; cotrimoxazole.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diagnosis. Modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain of stool: acid-fast pink-red oocysts; also immunofluorescence and coproantigens.

title: List the coccidia and their shared cycle.
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: List the coccidia and their shared cycle.
body.back: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora; schizogony (asexual), gamogony (sexual), sporogony (oocyst in stool).
C. hominis, C. parvum; mammals; oocysts resistant to chlorine; hands, water, food; waterborne epidemics.
Immunocompetent: incubation 3-12 days, self-limited watery diarrhoea 1-2 weeks. Immunocompromised (CD4 < 100): chronic choleriform, biliary and lung spread, death.
Stool: modified Ziehl-Neelsen (pink oocysts), IFD (apple-green), coproantigen ELISA; duodenal aspirate, BAL, biopsy.
ART in AIDS; paromomycin, azithromycin, nitazoxanide (partial); spontaneous healing in immunocompetent; rehydration and nutrition.
Tropical, strictly human; immature oocysts; berries, basil; watery traveller's diarrhoea; orange-red on ZN; cotrimoxazole.
Tropical, human, opportunistic; watery diarrhoea with fever; ZN; cotrimoxazole (ciprofloxacin, pyrimethamine).
Colonic protozoan, several forms; pathogenic when > 5/field, in children, elderly, HIV; metronidazole, cotrimoxazole if failure.

body.back: Capsular antigen. Soluble polysaccharide antigen by latex agglutination in CSF, serum, BAL, urine; used for diagnosis and follow-up.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: CNS tropism. CSF is a good culture medium with weaker defences: subacute meningoencephalitis with headache and cranial nerve palsies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Treatment. Induction amphotericin B + flucytosine for 2 weeks, consolidation fluconazole 400 mg, maintenance 200-400 mg.
Cosmopolitan mycosis due to encapsulated Cryptococcus neoformans, exogenous, with CNS tropism (meningoencephalitis) and possible lung, skin, bone, visceral forms.
Var. grubii and neoformans (A, D; cosmopolitan; soil, bird droppings); var. gattii (B, C; tropical; eucalyptus).
HIV with CD4 < 100 (AIDS-defining), long-term steroids, haematological malignancies, transplants, chemotherapy, sarcoidosis.
Insidious fever, headache, irritability, cranial nerve palsies, then meningeal syndrome; severity: seizures, coma, deficit, papilloedema (raised ICP).
Lung (often silent; nodules, infiltrates), skin (umbilicated pustules), bone, disseminated (liver, spleen, marrow, prostate).
Clear, high pressure, 10-100 lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose; may be normal in AIDS.
India ink (capsule), culture on Sabouraud without actidione at 37 °C, urease +, capsular antigen by latex in CSF/serum/BAL/urine.

title: Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis in HIV?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis in HIV?
body.back: Amphotericin B 0.7-1 mg/kg + flucytosine 100 mg/kg for 2 weeks; fluconazole 400 mg to week 10; maintenance 200-400 mg until immune recovery.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antigen and DNA. Rapid immunochromatographic or ELISA coproantigen tests; PCR for sensitivity, multiplex and species identification.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immunology. Ab or Ag in serum/CSF; screening (sensitive) + confirmation (specific); rising titre 15 days apart.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Special techniques. Ziehl-Neelsen for Cryptosporidium/Cyclospora, Kato for egg counts, Baermann for Strongyloides larvae, Graham scotch test for pinworm.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Parasitological stool exam. Gold standard for intestinal parasites: macroscopy, fresh exam, Lugol/MIF staining, two concentration methods; repeat 3 times.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thick drop. Concentration technique; WHO reference for malaria; also trypanosomes and microfilariae.

body.back: Thin smear. Giemsa/MGG; species identification and parasitaemia as % of red cells (Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma).
A technique adapted to each parasite; one negative exam excludes nothing (3 exams); sample quality (fresh stool, patient preparation).

title: Patient preparation and sampling for PES?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Patient preparation and sampling for PES?
body.back: 3-day low-residue diet, stop charcoal/oils/barium; whole fresh stool, sealed; formed ≤ 12 h, diarrhoeal ≤ 1 h or MIF; lab < 3 h.
Fresh exam, staining (Lugol, haematoxylin, MIF), concentration (physical: Willis; diphasic: Bailenger, Ritchie), special techniques.
Ziehl-Neelsen: Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora. Kato: helminth egg count. Baermann: Strongyloides larvae. Scotch test: pinworm.
Parasites not shed in stool, perianal eggs, dead ends; false positives (starch, pollen, spores, cells); time, expertise, low sensitivity.
Thin: species, stage, parasitaemia (%). Thick: concentration, WHO reference for malaria, trypanosomes, microfilariae.
Plasmodium: thin + thick. Leishmania, Toxoplasma: thin. Microfilariae: fresh, thick, leukoconcentration. Trypanosomes: fresh, thick, triple centrifugation.
IgM < 10 days, no placenta; IgG from ~1 week later, plateau, persists, crosses placenta; IgA local; IgE in helminthiases.
Direct diagnosis impossible (larval migration, hepatic amoebiasis, dead ends), follow-up (hydatid), congenital toxoplasmosis, fungal antigens, epidemiology.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Invasion phase. Weeks 1-4: larvae cross the liver causing toxi-infectious hepatitis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Infective form. Encysted metacercariae on wild watercress or dandelion, eaten raw.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intermediate host. The freshwater snail Lymnaea truncatula, where larval stages multiply.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: State phase. From 3 months: adults in bile ducts cause inflammation, hyperplasia, cholangitis, pseudolithiasis.
Trematodes: unsegmented leaf-shaped flatworms, 2 suckers, incomplete gut, mostly hermaphrodite, indirect cycle with freshwater snail, operculated non-embryonated eggs.

title: How are humans infected with flukes?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: How are humans infected with flukes?
body.back: Orally: metacercariae on wild watercress or dandelion; raw fish, crabs, crayfish.
Adults in bile ducts of sheep/cattle → eggs in faeces → snail Lymnaea truncatula → cercariae → metacercariae on watercress → ingestion.
Invasion (1-4 weeks): transhepatic migration, toxi-infectious hepatitis. State (≥ 3 months): adults in bile ducts, cholangitis, obstruction, pseudolithiasis.
Eggs in stool/bile from ~3 months (flotation, Kato, duodenal aspirate); serology (IFI, ELISA) from 3 weeks, > 90% sensitive, useful for follow-up.
Opisthorchis/Clonorchis (raw fish, Asia), Dicrocoelium (ants; transit eggs), Paragonimus (crabs; mimics TB), intestinal flukes (Asia, Egypt).
Avoid wild watercress, water chestnuts, undercooked fish and crustaceans.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Giardia cyst. Oval, thick-walled, 4 nuclei; resists bleach; the infective form.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Giardiasis. Attaches to duodenal and jejunal enterocytes: villous atrophy, fat and B12 malabsorption.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Giardia trophozoite. Pear-shaped, bilaterally symmetrical, 2 nuclei, 4 pairs of flagella; 'falling leaf' motility.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Treatment. Nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, tinidazole, secnidazole); treat sexual partners in trichomoniasis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Trichomonas vaginalis. Pear-shaped, 4 anterior flagella and an undulating membrane; no cyst; sexually transmitted.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Trichomoniasis. Women: vaginitis with frothy greenish foul discharge, pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia; men often asymptomatic urethritis.

title: Which intestinal flagellates exist and which is pathogenic?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Which intestinal flagellates exist and which is pathogenic?
body.back: Giardia intestinalis (pathogenic), Chilomastix mesnili, Trichomonas intestinalis, Enteromonas hominis, Embadomonas intestinalis (well tolerated).
Trophozoite: pear-shaped, bilateral, 2 nuclei, 4 pairs of flagella, falling-leaf motion. Cyst: oval, thick wall, 4 nuclei, infective, resistant.
Attachment to duodenal/jejunal enterocytes → villous atrophy, brush border loss; nutrient and bile acid capture → fat, vitamin and B12 malabsorption.
90% carriers; incubation 7 days; diarrhoea 5-10/day, cramps, flatulence, steatorrhoea, weight loss, failure to thrive, pale foul stools.
3 stool exams (saline, Lugol, concentration), duodenal aspirate/biopsy, coproantigens; metronidazole 5-7 days or single-dose tinidazole/secnidazole; control at 10 days.
Pear-shaped, central nucleus, 4 anterior flagella, posterior flagellum with undulating membrane; no cyst.
Women: vaginitis, frothy green foul discharge, pruritus, burning, dysuria, dyspareunia. Men: urethra/prostate, often latent urethritis.
Vaginal swab (no lubricant) or male morning secretions/urine; fresh saline exam, Giemsa; metronidazole 10 days or single-dose tinidazole/ornidazole; treat both partners.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hookworms. Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus suck blood from the duodenal mucosa.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Migration. Heart, lungs, trachea, then swallowed: Löffler syndrome with cough and high eosinophilia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Malignant strongyloidiasis. Hyperinfection in immunocompromised patients, above all on long-term corticosteroids; often fatal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Entry. Barefoot walking, farming, gardening, mining; itchy dermatitis at the entry site.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Infective larvae. In warm, damp soil enriched by human faeces; attracted by moisture and heat.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Strongyloides stercoralis. Parthenogenetic females in the duodenum; endogenous autoinfection lets infection persist 30+ years.

title: Which nematodes infect through the skin?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Which nematodes infect through the skin?
body.back: Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus) and Strongyloides stercoralis.
Encysted L3 larvae in warm, humid, faeces-enriched mud; barefoot walking, farming, gardening, mines; larvae attracted by moisture and heat.
Skin penetration → blood → heart → lungs → trachea → swallowed → duodenum (L4) → adult.
Skin: dermatitis, pruritus, miner's itch. Invasion: cough, dysphonia, Löffler, eosinophilia 50%. State: duodenal signs, iron-deficiency anaemia.
Stool (Willis, Kato), coproculture; albendazole 400 mg single dose, mebendazole 3 days, pyrantel; iron and folate.
Indirect sexual (free-living generation in soil), direct asexual (L1 → L3 outside), endogenous autoinfection (inside the host).
Skin pruritus, Löffler syndrome, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, larva currens; malignant form under steroids.
Saw-tooth eosinophilia 50-60%; rhabditoid larvae in stool, Baermann, coproculture; ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose or albendazole 3 days.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Definitive host. Adult Echinococcus (3-6 mm; scolex with 4 suckers and 2 rows of hooks; 3 segments) in the dog's intestine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Locations. Liver 50-60%, lung 30-40%, kidney 1.5-5%, others ~1% (bone, brain, heart).
Cosmopolitan rural zoonosis: development in humans and herbivores of the larva of Echinococcus granulosus, whose adult lives in the dog's intestine.
Dog: definitive host and reservoir. Herbivores (sheep): intermediate hosts. Humans: accidental intermediate hosts (dead end).

title: Why is hydatidosis endemic in Morocco?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Why is hydatidosis endemic in Morocco?
body.back: Pastoral herding, untreated farm and stray dogs, unburied carcasses, clandestine/family/festival slaughter with offal to dogs, poor hand and food hygiene.
3-6 mm; scolex with 4 suckers and 2 rows of hooklets; short neck; 3 segments, the last full of eggs.
Pericyst (host), ectocyst (acellular cuticle), germinal endocyst (brood capsules, protoscolices, fluid), hydatid sand.
Liver 50-60% (compression, rupture, anaphylaxis, abscess, jaundice), lung 30-40% (vomica, abscess), kidney 1.5-5% (hydaturia), others ~1%.
CL, CE1 simple unilocular, CE2 multivesicular, CE3 detached membranes/daughter cysts, CE4 degenerative (ball of wool), CE5 calcified.
Screen: ELISA + HAI (> 85%); confirm: Western blot 17 kDa; post-op titres rise at 4-6 weeks then negative in 12-24 months.
Surgery (~90% cure) + albendazole; PAIR for CE1/CE3a ≤ 10 cm; drainage > 10 cm; albendazole for small/multiple; watch and wait for CE4-5.
Veterinary control, incinerate offal, stop clandestine slaughter, deworm dogs with praziquantel, keep dogs out of slaughterhouses, hand and vegetable hygiene.

body.back: Short direct cycle. Monoxenous, no passage through the environment: Entamoeba, Enterobius.
A eukaryotic infectious agent that develops temporarily or permanently at the expense of another eukaryotic living being (the host), harming but not immediately killing it.
Protozoa (intestinal, blood/tissue, urogenital) and metazoa: helminths (nematodes, cestodes, trematodes) and arthropods.
Parasitism: one benefits, host harmed. Commensalism: one benefits, other unaffected (C. albicans, E. coli amoeba). Symbiosis: both benefit (lichen).
Facultative (fly larvae), accidental (human and Echinococcus), obligate temporary (tick) or permanent (louse).
Humans only (ascariasis); mainly animals (trichinosis, hydatid cyst); mainly humans with animals in the cycle (taeniasis).
Direct contact, ingestion, inhalation, skin penetration, sexual, transplacental, insect bite.

title: Definitive host, intermediate host, vector, reservoir?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Definitive host, intermediate host, vector, reservoir?
body.back: DH: adult/sexual forms. IH: larval/asexual forms. Vector: actively transmits (often insect). Reservoir: maintains the parasite in nature.
Short direct (amoeba), long direct (Ancylostoma), indirect/heteroxenous (Taenia, filariae), dead end (dog hookworm in humans).
Human-only, eggs on hands/bedding/air, adults in 2-4 weeks; evening anal pruritus; Graham scotch test; albendazole repeated at 15-21 days + household measures.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cutaneous leishmaniasis. L. major (rural, wet, multiple, fast healing) and L. tropica (urban, dry, single, slow) in Morocco.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vector. Female sandfly (2-5 mm, hairy, V-shaped wings), active at dusk and night above 19 °C; painful bite; injects promastigotes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Amastigote. 2-6 µm, aflagellate, intracellular in macrophages of the mononuclear phagocyte system.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis. New World L. braziliensis: destruction of nose, palate, pharynx.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reservoirs. Dogs (L. infantum), rodents (L. major), humans (L. tropica, L. donovani).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Visceral leishmaniasis. L. infantum in children around the Mediterranean: fever, pallor, splenomegaly, pancytopenia; fatal without treatment.
Anthropozoonoses due to flagellate protozoa Leishmania, obligate intracellular in macrophages, transmitted by sandflies; WHO priority disease.
Promastigote (15-25 µm, flagellated, sandfly gut/culture), amastigote (2-6 µm, aflagellate, intracellular in mammals).
2-5 mm hairy yellow midge, hunched, V wings, active dusk/night > 19 °C, silent flight, painful bite, larvae in damp soil.
Dog: L. infantum. Rodents: L. major. Humans: L. tropica, L. donovani.
Child; fever, pallor, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, nodes, weight loss; pancytopenia, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, ESR 80-100.
Amastigotes on MGG in bone marrow (sternal/iliac), NNN culture; ELISA, WB, rK39 rapid test; PCR.

title: L. tropica vs L. major cutaneous forms?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: L. tropica vs L. major cutaneous forms?
body.back: Tropica: urban, human reservoir, dry, single, slow (> 1 year). Major: rural, rodents, wet, multiple, inflamed, heals < 6 months.
Diffuse (aethiopica, mexicana, amazonensis; nodules, resistant), post-kala-azar dermal, mucocutaneous espundia (braziliensis).

title: Treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis in Morocco?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis in Morocco?
body.back: Local care; Glucantime intralesional (< 5 lesions, < 4 cm) or IM 20 mg/kg/d (> 5 or > 4 cm); paromomycin, cryo/thermotherapy; CI: > 50 y, pregnancy, organ failure.
Meglumine antimoniate 60 mg/kg/d IM 28 days; amphotericin B for relapse; liposomal amphotericin B; monitor ECG, blood, organs.

body.back: Inoculation. Female Anopheles bites at night (11 p.m.-4 a.m.) and injects sporozoites.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Malaria attack. Synchronous release of merozoites and toxic products causes chills, fever and sweats.

body.back: Gametocytes. Sexual forms in the blood, infective for mosquitoes; their presence after treatment does not justify retreatment.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hepatic phase. Asexual multiplication in hepatocytes; P. vivax and P. ovale leave dormant hypnozoites (late relapses).

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Sporogonic cycle. Sexual reproduction in the mosquito ends with sporozoites in the salivary glands.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Erythrocytic cycle. Merozoites invade red cells, feed on haemoglobin and multiply; P. falciparum infects red cells of all ages.
Plasmodium (parasite), humans (reservoir; premunition), female Anopheles (vector; night bites, fresh water).

title: Five Plasmodium species and fever rhythm?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Five Plasmodium species and fever rhythm?
body.back: P. falciparum (48 h, severe), P. vivax and P. ovale (48 h, relapses), P. malariae (72 h), P. knowlesi (24 h, SE Asia).
Heteroxenous: sporozoites → liver (± hypnozoites) → erythrocytic cycle (ring, trophozoite, schizont, merozoites) → gametocytes → mosquito sexual cycle.
Control from 1965; last indigenous case 2004; WHO elimination certificate 2010; imported cases, prevent reintroduction.
Incubation 7-21 days; fever, chills, sweats, headache, myalgia, digestive signs; anaemia, thrombocytopenia.
Coma (GCS ≤ 9), seizures, Hb < 7 g/dL, hypoglycaemia, acidosis, respiratory distress, renal failure, haemoglobinuria, DIC, pulmonary oedema, jaundice, lactate ↑, parasitaemia ≥ 4%.
Cytoadherence and sequestration of P. falciparum-infected red cells in brain capillaries → obstruction, hypoxia, toxic release.
Thick drop (sensitive, WHO reference), thin smear (species, stage, parasitaemia), RDT (HRP2, pLDH; never alone), PCR (most sensitive), serology (not diagnostic).
Falciparum: artemether-lumefantrine 3 days + primaquine 0.25 mg/kg; vivax/ovale: chloroquine + primaquine; malariae: chloroquine; severe: IV artesunate or quinine.
Treatment and chemoprophylaxis; repellents, clothing, insecticide-treated nets; vector control of breeding sites and adults.

body.back: Pityriasis capitis. Non-inflammatory scalp hyperkeratosis producing dandruff, no hair loss.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Malassezia. Small (3-6 µm) lipid-dependent yeasts living in hair follicles, feeding on sebum fatty acids; urease positive.
Benign, frequent, recurrent skin mycoses due to overgrowth of Malassezia, lipophilic keratinophilic commensal yeasts of sebaceous skin.
Malassezia needs free fatty acids from sebum; sebum rises at puberty and falls with age.
Heat, summer, sweating (sauna, sport), oils and fatty cosmetics, Cushing's, pregnancy, contraceptives, corticosteroids.
Pityriasis versicolor, pityriasis capitis (dandruff), seborrhoeic dermatitis, pityrosporum folliculitis.
Round well-limited macules around follicles, merging into polycyclic sheets; pink-brown then achromic; fine scaling (chip sign); trunk, root of limbs.
Wood's lamp yellow-green; scotch test or scraping with methylene blue: grape-like clusters of spores and short filaments; culture unnecessary.
Topical azoles/ciclopirox/terbinafine 2-3 weeks or ketoconazole gel once; systemic azoles for diffuse/recurrent; not contagious, relapses, pigment recovers slowly.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Trichuriasis. Colic, diarrhoea; heavy infection: dysentery, tenesmus, rectal prolapse, hypochromic anaemia.
E. vermicularis; human reservoir; caecum/appendix; female lays 5,000-15,000 embryonated eggs at the anus at night; short direct cycle, adults in 2-4 weeks.
Evening anal pruritus, insomnia, irritability; Graham scotch test; albendazole repeated at 15-21 days, treat household, hygiene measures.

Eggs in stool or spontaneous worm; albendazole or mebendazole; faecal hazard control.
Whip-shaped (thin anterior 2/3); eggs lemon-shaped with a mucous plug at each pole, double shell, unembryonated.
Colic, diarrhoea/constipation, weight loss; heavy: profuse diarrhoea, tenesmus, rectal bleeding and prolapse, appendicitis, iron-deficiency anaemia.

Opportunistic pneumonia due to the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii; airborne, human reservoir; first AIDS complication before ART.
HIV with CD4 < 200, cancers, haemopathies, malnutrition, prematurity, T-cell deficiency, steroids, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants.
Dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, hypoxaemia (SaO₂ < 90%), normal auscultation; bilateral alveolar-interstitial infiltrates, CT ground glass.
Orientation: ↑ LDH, hypoxaemia, low lymphocytes, CD4 < 200. Certainty: BAL/aspirate/biopsy with MGG or Grocott, PCR (no culture).
Cotrimoxazole (SMX 75 + TMP 15 mg/kg/d) 21 days; alternatives atovaquone, pentamidine; steroids if PaO₂ < 70 mmHg.
Cotrimoxazole daily (alternatives dapsone-pyrimethamine, pentamidine aerosols, atovaquone); primary if CD4 < 200; secondary after any episode; stop if CD4 > 200 for 3 months.

Tachyzoite (acute, multiplying, crosses placenta), tissue cyst with bradyzoites (chronic, persistent), oocyst (cat faeces, sporulates in soil).
DH: cats. IH: humans, animals (dead end in humans). Routes: meat cysts, oocysts (vegetables, water, litter), transplacental, transplant, transfusion.
1st: low transmission, severe damage (abortion). 3rd: high transmission, mild lesions.
80% asymptomatic; 15-20% cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, asthenia; mononucleosis syndrome; heals without sequelae.
Severe (hydrocephalus/microcephaly, calcifications, seizures, chorioretinitis), benign (attenuated), latent (80%, later chorioretinitis).
IgG+IgM−: immune. IgG−IgM−: non-immune, monthly follow-up. IgG−IgM+ then IgG+: seroconversion. IgG+IgM+: avidity or repeat at 3 weeks.

title: Hygiene advice for seronegative pregnant women?
subject: subj:parasito

body.front: Hygiene advice for seronegative pregnant women?
body.back: Well-cooked or previously frozen meat, wash fruit and vegetables, wash hands, avoid cat litter; no vaccine.

Pregnancy: spiramycin (fetus uninfected) or pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine (infected). Newborn: P-S + folinic acid 1 year. AIDS: cotrimoxazole prophylaxis CD4 < 100. Ocular: P + sulfadiazine or clindamycin.
